name: RocksDB integrated BlobDB
baseline: stock RocksDB (leveled compaction, no blob files)
workload: db_bench-based write/overwrite/point-lookup/range-scan workloads across six value sizes (1KB-1MB) comparing enable_blob_files=true (integrated BlobDB) against leveled and universal compaction without blob files, on RocksDB v6.18.1-equivalent
claimed_speedup: Initial load 2.3x-4.7x faster with write amp near the theoretical minimum (1.0-1.02 vs 1.6); overwrite workload 2.1x-3.5x higher throughput and 75-78% lower write amp vs leveled; point-lookup/write mix 83-88% lower write amp; range-scan/write mix 88-90% lower write amp; up to 1.4x higher read throughput vs leveled (5.6x vs universal) for larger values; new BlobDB implementation 4.6x faster than legacy StackableDB BlobDB without WAL, 2.3x with WAL, on single-threaded random writes with 1KB values
hardware: 18-core Skylake DE CPU @ 1.6GHz (hyperthreading enabled), 64GB RAM, 512GB boot SSD, 2x1.88TB NVMe SSDs in RAID0
stars_or_usage: 32.1k stars; used in production at Meta, MySQL/MyRocks, CockroachDB, TiKV, and others
tradeoffs: Blob files add space amplification and require separate blob garbage collection; best suited to workloads with large values (key-value separation); overhead is not worthwhile for small values.
caveats: First-party RocksDB engineering blog post, not an independent benchmark; CPU model and RocksDB version are stated but exact db_bench command lines and compiler/build flags are not (tool described only as 'a customized version of our standard benchmark suite'), which caps this at tier C rather than A. Numbers are from 2021 (RocksDB v6.18.1) and may not reflect current defaults.

name: FastPLBF (fast PLBF / fast PLBF++)
workload: Constructing a partitioned learned-Bloom-filter data structure from real-world datasets (Malicious URLs dataset, EMBER malware dataset), varying segment count N and region count k, measuring wall-clock construction time versus resulting memory usage / false positive rate
claimed_speedup: fast PLBF constructs the same data structure as PLBF up to 233x faster with identical memory efficiency; fast PLBF++ constructs it up to 761x faster with almost identical (slightly worse) memory efficiency
tradeoffs: Reference Python implementation only, no production/C++ port; the speedup is an algorithmic construction-time complexity reduction (O(N^2 k) or O(Nk log N + Nk^2) vs PLBF's O(N^3 k)), most pronounced at large N; fast PLBF++ trades a small amount of memory efficiency for its larger speedup.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (NeurIPS 2023) but the paper states no CPU/hardware details for the construction-time numbers, so it falls short of tier A despite public code and real datasets. Comparison is against the authors' own PLBF reimplementation in the same repo, not an independent PLBF benchmark.

name: NNG (nanomsg-next-generation)
workload: Independent PUB/SUB benchmarking suite comparing ZeroMQ (libzmq 4.3.4), NanoMsg (libnanomsg 1.1.5) and NNG (libnng 1.9.0) across In-Process, Inter-Process, and TCP-loopback transports, varying message size (1KB-512KB) and subscriber count, on a single host
claimed_speedup: For Inter-Process communication, NNG shows higher throughput than NanoMsg for the two largest message sizes; for TCP communication, NanoMsg throughput peaks around 1.5 GB/s at 128KB then decreases, while NNG throughput monotonically increases and surpasses NanoMsg for large payloads, peaking around 2 GB/s; NNG also becomes more CPU-efficient than ZeroMQ for larger Inter-Process payloads
hardware: Intel Xeon w3-2435, 8 cores @ 3.1GHz, 64GB RAM; single host, loopback interface for TCP transport
tradeoffs: NNG is generally NOT the fastest of the three: the paper's overall conclusion is that ZeroMQ delivers the highest throughput and NanoMsg the best CPU efficiency across most configurations and transports; NNG's wins are narrow (large-payload throughput vs NanoMsg in Inter-Process/TCP, and CPU efficiency vs ZeroMQ at large Inter-Process payloads). NNG also shows worse latency scaling with subscriber count than the other two.
caveats: Independent third-party arXiv preprint (2508.07934, Aug 2025) with a public benchmark-suite repo (github.com/hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark) and stated CPU model/library versions, but no compiler/build flags are given, capping it at tier B rather than A. Not confirmed to be the IEEE SRDS 2025 paper referenced in the lead (venue not stated as SRDS; appears to be an unpublished preprint under cs.DC/cs.NI). The headline finding across the paper is that NNG usually loses to ZeroMQ and often to NanoMsg; the qualifying win here is a specific large-payload throughput result, not overall superiority.
